name: Stately
tagline: Visual editor, simulator and code generator for XState state machines.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The engine underneath is XState, which is open source and free, so you are not paying for the hard part. You are paying for the canvas: drag states around, draw transitions, simulate a machine by clicking through it, and keep the diagram in sync with real TypeScript. An agent can build a local React Flow editor that emits XState v5 config and replays events against a live actor in one sitting, and for flat or lightly nested machines that is genuinely useful. Where it falls apart is the unglamorous stuff: sane auto-layout for parallel and deeply nested states, parsing existing machine source back into a graph, generated test paths, and shared diagrams your teammates can comment on. Fine for solo modeling, weak as a team artifact.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you drag states and transitions on a canvas, export a valid XState v5 machine config, and step through it against a running actor to watch state and context change.
requirements: React Flow or similar canvas library
whatYouLose: Code to diagram round-tripping: parsing an existing TypeScript machine back onto a canvas is the genuinely hard part and your build will not do it
Auto-layout that does not look like spaghetti once you add parallel and nested states
Shared, commentable diagrams that non-engineers can actually read
Generated test paths and coverage from the machine definition
Type-aware editing of actions, guards and actors with autocomplete against your real codebase
moatNotes: The moat is not the state machine format, that is public. It is the years of graph layout and editor ergonomics that make a 40 state machine legible.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because state charts only pay off when other people look at them, and a diagram nobody else can open is just a slower way of writing code. Teams pay for the shared canvas, the layout that stays readable as the machine grows, and the round trip that keeps the picture honest when someone edits the TypeScript. A solo developer modeling one flow can skip all of that and be fine. A team that adopted XState as a communication tool cannot.
notes: XState is free; the canvas is the product, and the canvas is mostly layout math.
prompt:
Build a local visual state machine editor and simulator. No accounts, no backend, no telemetry.

Stack: Vite + React + TypeScript, React Flow for the canvas, xstate v5 and @xstate/react for the runtime, Tailwind for styling. Persist to localStorage plus explicit JSON import/export. Everything runs with `npm run dev`.

Layout: three panes. Left is a machine list. Center is the canvas. Right is an inspector that switches between the selected node, the selected edge, and a simulator tab.

Canvas requirements:
- Add, rename, move and delete states. Mark one state as initial, mark states as final.
- Draw transitions by dragging between state handles. Each transition has an event name, an optional guard name, and an ordered list of action names.
- Support entry and exit action names per state.
- Support one level of nested states via a compound state that can be expanded inline. Do not attempt parallel states.
- Free-form context editing as a raw JSON textarea, no schema builder.

Code generation:
- Live panel that renders the current graph as a valid `createMachine({...})` call for xstate v5, formatted TypeScript, with a copy button.
- Guards and actions are emitted as string references, with a stubbed `setup({ guards, actions })` block listing every name used so the output pastes into a real project and compiles.
- One-way only. Do not try to parse TypeScript back into the graph.

Simulator:
- Instantiate the current machine with @xstate/react, highlight the active state node on the canvas, list currently available events as clickable buttons, and show a scrolling event log with the context after each transition.
- Guards evaluate as always-true stubs in simulation, and say so in the UI.
- Reset button.

Explicitly out of scope: auto-layout, collaboration, sharing links, test path generation, parallel states, actor invocation, and anything that needs a server.

Include a README covering the data model, the limits above, and how to paste generated machines into an existing project.
